Teacher has checked actual Listening Screener and review states privately.
Approved recording IELTS-14-L1 with verified hash. Without it this lesson is not releasable; see Plan B.

objectives.text: Follow decisions in a three-speaker discussion where suggestions are made, rejected and revised.
Answer 'choose TWO' questions by checking each option against what is finally agreed, not what is first mentioned.
Match items to decisions (matching features) while keeping track of answers that arrive late.

levels.foundation: Speaker names written in the margin with one adjective each after the introduction; teacher-controlled second play with pauses after each decision, recorded as support.
levels.core: Answer all eight questions after one play.
levels.extension: For each matching item, write the option that was suggested first and then rejected or changed, if any.
levels.high_band: After one play, explain in two sentences why Josh's plan for the recommendations changed, using the reason Amira gives.

blocks.title: Choose TWO: what was finally agreed?
blocks.mode: Teacher-led mini-model; read aloud live from the slide
blocks.instructions: Listen to your teacher read the short exchange once. Which TWO things will the students bring?

stimulus.title: Mini-model (teacher reads aloud)
paragraphs: A: Should we bring a laptop and a projector? B: The room has a projector already. But bring the laptop. A: And the printed handouts? B: Yes, definitely. Oh, and the speakers? A: The room has those too.

items.prompt: Which TWO will the students bring? A laptop / B projector / C handouts / D speakers
items.reason: The projector and speakers are rejected because the room already has them; the laptop and handouts are confirmed.

blocks.title: Preparing a presentation
blocks.mode: Guided listening practice: one play under practice conditions, then teacher-controlled review
blocks.instructions: Questions 1-2: choose TWO letters, A-E. Questions 3-6: what do the speakers decide about each part of the presentation? Choose the correct letter, A-F, from the list (A shorten it; B add examples; C remove it; D move it to the start; E ask the tutor again; F keep it unchanged). Questions 7-8: choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

stimulus.title: Recording IELTS-14-L1 transcript (teacher-private)
paragraphs: PROFESSOR GRANT: Come in, Amira, Josh. So, how's the presentation coming along?
JOSH: Getting there, I think. The survey was harder than we expected, though.
PROFESSOR GRANT: In what way?
AMIRA: Well, we were worried at first that we wouldn't get enough responses, but in the end thirty-two businesses replied, which was more than we needed.
JOSH: The real problem was the wording. Several owners thought 'engagement' meant how many followers they had, so their answers to question four don't really tell us anything.
AMIRA: And we sent it out too late. Most replies came in last week, so we've had very little time to analyse them.
PROFESSOR GRANT: Those are both useful things to mention when you discuss the limitations. Now, let's go through the structure. You've got a background section first?
AMIRA: Yes, but it's over four minutes long at the moment.
PROFESSOR GRANT: That's far too much for a fifteen-minute talk. I'd cut it to about one minute. The audience will know the basics.
JOSH: OK, we'll shorten it. Then we have the survey results.
PROFESSOR GRANT: What's the most surprising finding?
AMIRA: That the smallest businesses, the ones with only one or two staff, post more often than the larger ones.
PROFESSOR GRANT: That's a strong hook. Why not open with it, rather than burying it in the middle?
JOSH: Good idea. So the results go at the start.
AMIRA: What about the slide on the history of social media? I spent quite a long time on that.
PROFESSOR GRANT: I can see it was a lot of work, but it doesn't connect to your question. I'd leave it out altogether.
AMIRA: Fair enough.
JOSH: And the recommendations at the end? We were going to leave them as they are.
PROFESSOR GRANT: They're sensible, but rather general. Each one would be more convincing with a real example from one of the businesses you surveyed.
JOSH: Right, we can do that. By the way, I heard the deadline had been moved to next Friday.
PROFESSOR GRANT: That's for the marketing group, I'm afraid. Yours is still this Thursday, as planned.
JOSH: Ah. OK, Thursday it is.
PROFESSOR GRANT: And who's presenting which part?
JOSH: I was going to do the results and the recommendations, and Amira the background.
AMIRA: Actually, since the background is now so short, wouldn't it make more sense for me to do the recommendations as well? I interviewed most of the owners, so I know the examples.
JOSH: That makes sense. You take the recommendations, then.
PROFESSOR GRANT: Good. Send me your slides by Wednesday morning if you'd like comments.

items.prompt: Questions 1-2. Which TWO problems did the students have with their survey?
options: C  it was sent out too late
E  businesses refused to take part
items.evidence: And we sent it out too late
items.reason: B: owners misunderstood 'engagement' in question four. C: replies arrived late. A is mentioned as a worry but did not happen (thirty-two replied). D and E are not mentioned.

items.evidence: I'd cut it to about one minute
So the results go at the start
items.reason: The surprising finding becomes the opening hook.
Amira accepts: 'Fair enough.' Effort spent on it is not a reason to keep it.

items.evidence: Each one would be more convincing with a real example
items.reason: F (keep unchanged) was the students' original plan, but they agree to add examples.

items.evidence: Yours is still this Thursday, as planned
items.reason: Next Friday is the marketing group's deadline; Wednesday morning is for optional slide comments.
Josh planned to present them, but Amira takes them because she knows the examples. The answer comes late in the conversation.

blocks.support: Foundation: after the introduction, write A, J and PG in the margin with one word to remember each voice. A second, paused play is allowed after the first attempt and recorded as support.
blocks.extension: For Questions 3-6, write the option first suggested or assumed, if different from the answer.
blocks.high_band: Explain in two sentences why the plan for the recommendations changed.

stages.title: Opening challenge: choose TWO
stages.student: Listen to a short exchange read aloud once and choose TWO.
stages.teacher: Read once at natural speed. Reveal. Establish the rule: in 'choose TWO', every option may be mentioned; only two are finally agreed.
stages.say: Mentioned is not the same as chosen.
stages.check: Learners can say why the projector is wrong.

stages.title: Strategy: tracking decisions
stages.student: Copy the decision signals: 'I'd...', 'Why not...?', 'Good idea', 'That makes sense', 'Fair enough', 'Actually...'. Underline the key word in each option for Questions 1-8.
stages.teacher: Explain that in Part 3, a suggestion becomes an answer only when the speakers accept it. Foundation group prepares the speaker margin notes.
stages.say: Wait for the agreement: 'OK, we'll...', 'That makes sense', 'Fair enough'.
stages.check: Learners can name three agreement signals.

stages.title: Prepare for the recording
stages.student: Read Questions 1-8 during the reading time.
stages.teacher: The recording gives 30 seconds of reading time; allow one more minute. Do not pre-teach answers.
stages.say: Three speakers. Track who suggests and who decides.

stages.title: The tutorial: one play
stages.teacher: Play IELTS-14-L1 once without pausing. If audio fails, stop and use Plan B; never read the transcript as a substitute.
stages.say: Some answers come late. Keep listening to the end.

stages.title: Review: suggestions, decisions and late answers
stages.student: Check answers. For each wrong answer, write whether you chose a suggestion that was later changed, or missed a late answer.
stages.teacher: Reveal Q1-2, then Q3-6, then Q7-8. Focus on Q1-2 (A was a worry, not a problem), Q6 (F was the original plan) and Q8 (late change). Optional teacher-controlled second play for foundation learners, recorded as support.
stages.say: The final decision is the answer, even if it comes several lines later.
stages.check: Learners can explain the trap in Q6 and Q8.

stages.title: Transcript analysis (guided review)
stages.student: With the transcript handout (teacher-released after the first play), highlight each suggestion in one colour and each agreement in another for Questions 3-8.
stages.teacher: Distribute the transcript only now, as guided review. Model one example. Collect transcripts afterwards; they are not homework.
stages.say: See how each decision has two steps: a suggestion, then acceptance.
stages.check: Learners have highlighted at least four suggestion-decision pairs.

stages.title: Second listen without the transcript
stages.student: Listen once more without the transcript and notice the decisions as they happen.
stages.teacher: Play again as guided review. Record it as practice.
stages.say: Listen for the agreement signals you highlighted.
stages.check: Learners report noticing at least two decisions in real time.

stages.title: My listening log
stages.student: In the log at the end of the workbook, record each wrong answer and its trap type, and set one target.
stages.teacher: Note the trap types learners actually record. No band conversion.
stages.say: Your log shows which trap to practise.

stages.title: Exit ticket and homework
stages.student: Complete the exit ticket and take the homework sheet.
stages.teacher: Collect exit tickets and transcripts. Assign online practice only through the existing workflow. Record the fresh-check date.
stages.say: Next lesson: writing a complete Task 2 essay under time.
stages.check: Everyone knows the homework and check date.

exit_ticket: How I know a suggestion has become a decision:
What I do in 'choose TWO' questions:
My target for the next listening task:
homework: Listen to a discussion or interview in English with at least two speakers (5-10 minutes). Note one suggestion that was accepted and one that was rejected, with the words that showed it.
Write a six-line dialogue where a plan changes twice before the final decision. Swap with a partner next lesson.
Complete only the Brains Heist listening practice your teacher actually assigns.

blocks.title: Planning a field trip
blocks.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

stimulus.title: Recording IELTS-14-C1 transcript (teacher-private)
paragraphs: DR OKAFOR: So, the river field trip. Have you agreed on a date?
BEN: We'd thought about the twelfth, but the bus company is fully booked that day, so it'll be the nineteenth.
DR OKAFOR: Fine. And what are you each responsible for?
LUCY: I'm organising the equipment. We need water-testing kits, and the department only has four, so I've asked the chemistry lab to lend us another two.
BEN: I'll do the safety briefing. I was going to write a long document, but you said a short checklist would be better?
DR OKAFOR: Yes, people actually read a checklist. One page is plenty.
LUCY: What about lunch? Originally we said everyone should bring their own, but the café by the bridge offered us a discount.
DR OKAFOR: I'd still ask people to bring their own. The café is small, and twenty-five students would take ages to serve.
BEN: OK. And the report: is it individual or a group report?
DR OKAFOR: Each pair writes one report. Not individual, and not the whole group.
LUCY: How long should it be?
DR OKAFOR: Around two thousand words. Some students write much more, but that usually means they haven't selected the important results.

items.prompt: When will the field trip take place?
items.reason: The twelfth was rejected because the bus company is fully booked.

items.prompt: How many water-testing kits will they have?
items.evidence: I've asked the chemistry lab to lend us another two
items.reason: Four from the department plus two borrowed.

items.prompt: What form will the safety information take?
items.reason: The long document was Ben's original plan.

items.prompt: What will students do about lunch?
options: B  eat at the café by the bridge
C  buy food on the bus
items.evidence: I'd still ask people to bring their own
items.reason: The café discount is mentioned but rejected.
The tutor rules out the other two options explicitly.

items.prompt: What does Dr Okafor say about the length of the report?
options: A  Longer reports usually get better marks.
B  About two thousand words is appropriate.
C  There is no word limit.
items.reason: He warns that much longer reports usually lack selection, which contradicts A.
